criteria.rationale: The tests verify ordinary local graphs, but the assumption that every graph layer resides beside the primary chain is false for alternates. The 500-commit threshold is an explicit D1 policy choice, not a benchmark independently reproduced here.
Production changes introduce no shared mutable state or goroutines. Files are closed, and graph publication remains Git's responsibility. No new cancellation contract is introduced.
The new check uses existing finding and fix-registry contracts without changing report fields, MCP interfaces, or governance storage.
doctor.go adds an existing-schema check and registry action. CLI flags, report schema, existing fix behavior, and MCP contracts remain compatible.

D1 links the measured path-history traversal cost to R1-R3. Explicit doctor remediation writes changed-path filters while governance reads remain read-only; R4 prepares full-history CI checkouts before gates. This addresses the stated cause, subject to the graph-discovery defects.

The spec and runtime hints name the implemented Git command, threshold, explicit-fix behavior, and two CI placements. The pre-existing doctor performance issue remains explicitly tracked as spec follow-up F1.
The sealed test supports the ordinary R1-R3 path and CI inspection supports R4, but R3 fails for valid alternate-backed graphs. Coexisting graphs also expose the R1 failure in F3.
The implementation is confined to doctor diagnosis/remediation, CI preparation, and registered validation. It introduces neither automatic governance maintenance nor per-commit graph updates.

The fix invokes RawHistoryGit with fixed arguments and the selected project root. Its shared wrapper removes ambient Git redirection variables. Error output passes through existing doctor redaction; no new credentials, network access, or authority mechanism is introduced.

Reusing the existing fix registry and reading small graph headers is a proportionate implementation of D1. Documentation alone would not provide the required diagnostic; automatic writes would violate the read-only constraint. The approach remains sufficient only if its graph selection matches Git, requiring F2 and F3.

findings.action: Graph discovery ignores alternate object directories. Git can load a filtered graph entirely from an alternate, or resolve a split chain's base layers there, but this reader searches only the primary object directory and constructs every layer beside its chain file. A valid filtered repository therefore reports next instead of ok, violating R3. Follow Git's alternate lookup semantics and cover both alternate-only graphs and chains with alternate base layers.

The reader prefers a nonempty split chain over the monolithic commit-graph, whereas Git loads the monolithic graph first. When both exist, doctor can inspect an unused graph: an unfiltered monolithic graph plus a filtered chain reports ok although Git lacks active filters; the reverse reports an unnecessary remediation. Match Git's precedence and test coexistence.

The parser validates only the signature and nonzero chunk offsets before accepting BIDX and BDAT identifiers. Unsupported format/hash versions and a file truncated immediately after its chunk table can therefore report changedPaths=true even though Git rejects the graph. Validate supported header fields and chunk-table bounds against file size without reading chunk payloads; cover malformed headers and truncated files.

Every readCommitGraphState error suppresses the check. This conflates the intended non-repository/unborn-HEAD exclusions with permission failures, corrupt history, and unreadable graph metadata. For example, an inaccessible commit-graphs directory makes a long-history repository lose the finding and remediation entirely. Distinguish expected exclusions from operational failures and emit bounded actionable diagnostic context for the latter.
